planting.note: Set container-grown plants in spring into saturated to consistently wet, highly acidic sandy or peaty soil in full sun to partial shade; this pocosin and cypress-pond-margin shrub needs steady moisture and declines quickly if allowed to dry out or if soil pH rises much above 5.5.

directions: Myrtle-leaved St. John's-wort is a low, rounded evergreen shrub of pocosins, cypress-pond margins, and Carolina bay edges from North Carolina to Florida, instantly recognizable by its glaucous, blue-green, rounded leaves that clasp directly against reddish stems. Clusters of bright yellow, five-petaled flowers open through summer and draw a steady stream of native bees and small pollinators. Grow it in constantly wet, acidic, sandy-peaty soil in sun to light shade as a companion to fetterbush, zenobia, and inkberry in a rain garden or bog planting, and avoid any liming or runoff from concrete that could sweeten the soil. Light shaping after flowering keeps the naturally twiggy, mounding habit tidy without reducing next year's bloom.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery plugs in spring into saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic peaty or sandy soil in part sun to light shade, mimicking the pocosin-margin seeps and Carolina bay edges where this coarse clumping sedge is found from Virginia to the Gulf Coast.

directions: Spearfruit sedge forms broad, arching tufts of wide, grass-like leaves and takes its name from the narrow, lance-shaped fruiting bodies (perigynia) that line its flowering stalks in spring. It is native to blackwater seeps, pocosin margins, and the wet edges of Carolina bays across the southeastern coastal plain, where it roots into consistently saturated, acidic peat or sand. Use it as a coarse-textured anchor planting at the edge of a bog garden or rain garden pond, alongside pitcher plants and sundews that share the same wet, nutrient-poor conditions. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes and needs little care beyond cutting back old foliage in late winter.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)
Godfrey & Wooten, Aquatic and Wetland Plants of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into mucky, acidic, sandy soil kept constantly moist to shallowly flooded in full sun; this Xyris takes its name from its unusually broad, flattened, iris-like leaf fans, which make it one of the showiest yellow-eyed grasses for a Carolina bay pond margin or bog garden.

directions: Iris-leaf yellow-eyed grass grows a fan of wide, flattened, strongly ribbed leaves that resemble a miniature iris more than a typical wiry Xyris, topped in summer by small three-petaled yellow flowers that open one at a time from a hard, scaly cone-like spike. It occurs naturally in the mucky margins of Carolina bay ponds, cypress depressions, and wet pine flatwoods of the coastal plain, always in constantly saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor sand or peat. Grow it in full sun at the shallow edge of a bog garden or man-made pond where it will not dry out, pairing it with pipewort and sundews that share the same habitat. It needs no fertilizer and resents any liming or enriched garden soil.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring directly into shallow standing water or saturated acidic muck at a pond or bay margin in full sun; this sprawling beaksedge roots along floating or creeping stems and is best grown where water levels stay fairly constant.

directions: Narrowfruit horned beaksedge is a sprawling, semi-aquatic sedge that forms loose floating or rooted mats along the shallow, acidic margins of Carolina bay ponds and cypress depressions, with wiry stems bearing distinctive horn-tipped seed clusters in summer. In a garden setting it is best used at the flooded edge of a constructed bog pond or rain garden basin, where its arching stems can sprawl over the water surface alongside pipewort and bladderworts. It tolerates fluctuating water depth but performs best with at least a few inches of standing water through the growing season. Thin congested patches every year or two to keep the planting from becoming a dense monoculture.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)
Godfrey & Wooten, Aquatic and Wetland Plants of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Press small plugs or soil clumps into saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic sand or peat kept constantly wet to shallowly flooded in full sun; this terrestrial bladderwort carries its tiny prey traps underground and needs open, mossy ground free of competing vegetation.

directions: Southern bladderwort is a diminutive carnivorous plant of wet pine savannas, pocosin seeps, and Carolina bay pond margins, nearly invisible until its wiry, rush-like flower scapes push up small yellow snapdragon-shaped blooms on thin leafless stalks that rise above the mossy, saturated sand where its tiny underground bladder traps work unseen. Grow it in a shallow carnivorous-plant tray or bog-garden margin kept permanently damp with rainwater or distilled water, never fertilizer or tap water, alongside sundews and dwarf pitcher plants that share the same mineral-poor conditions. It spreads readily by seed and underground stolons once established in open, sunny, wet sand, forming a thin turf over several seasons. Avoid any potting mix containing compost, fertilizer, or lime, which quickly kill it.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Introduce small clumps into shallow, standing or saturated acidic water over sandy peat in full sun; this tiny free-floating-rooted bladderwort does best in a dedicated carnivorous bog tray or small container pool rather than mixed garden soil.

directions: Two-flowered bladderwort is a miniature aquatic carnivore of Carolina bay ponds, roadside ditches, and cypress pool margins, trapping tiny aquatic organisms with microscopic bladders strung along thread-fine, mostly submersed stems. Its small paired yellow flowers rise just above the water surface on short scapes in summer, giving the plant its common name. It thrives in shallow, still, acidic water with a sandy or peaty bottom and is best grown in a small tub or the flooded shelf of a bog garden rather than ordinary wet soil. Keep the water level steady and free of fertilizer runoff, since even modest nutrient enrichment allows algae to smother this slow-growing plant.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Set small rooted pieces into shallow, acidic, sandy-bottomed water or saturated peat in full sun; fibrous bladderwort roots lightly into the substrate rather than floating freely, so it suits the shallow flooded shelf of a bog garden better than deep open water.

directions: Fibrous bladderwort is a small, rooted aquatic carnivore found along the shallow, acidic margins of Carolina bay ponds and blackwater ditches, where fine, fibrous root-like stems anchor it in sandy peat while thread-fine foliage bears microscopic bladder traps for aquatic microfauna. Bright yellow, two-lipped flowers appear on short emergent stalks through the warm months, somewhat larger and showier than those of its close relatives. Grow it in the shallow, still-water margin of a constructed bog pond with a sandy or peaty bottom, kept free of fertilizer and competing floating weeds. It spreads slowly into loose colonies and pairs naturally with pipeworts, yellow-eyed grasses, and native pitcher plants in a southeastern bog display.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)
